title: Computer Vision
body:
Getting meaning out of a grid of numbers. An image is a [[Matrix]] of pixel intensities and nothing
else; the task is to answer questions a person answers instantly from it ("is there a face", "what
digit is this", "where does that object end") from the numbers alone.

**The hard part is the gap between the two.** The same object gives completely different pixel
values under a different light, angle, distance, or occlusion, while two different objects can give
nearly identical ones. There is no formula from pixels to meaning, which is exactly the
"you cannot write the algorithm" situation that [[MACHINE LEARNING]] exists for, and it is why
vision was one of the first places learning beat hand-written rules decisively.

## Three eras, and each is a note in the vault

| Era | Approach | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|
| Classical | hand-designed filters: edges, corners, gradients | [[Image Processing]] (MATH 2303) |
| Statistical | learn a linear basis from the data | [[Principal Component Analysis]], eigenfaces |
| Deep | learn non-linear local filters end to end | [[CNN]] |

The progression is one of **who designs the features.** A classical edge detector is a small
convolution kernel that a person wrote down; eigenfaces let [[Singular Value Decomposition]] pick a
basis from a set of face images, which is [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]] of a covariance matrix
and nothing more; a [[CNN]] learns the kernels themselves by [[Gradient Descent]]. Note that the
*operation* barely changes across all three: it is a filter slid over the image, taking a
[[Dot Product]] at each position. What changes is where the filter's numbers come from.

The pixels-to-vector problem is also why vision motivated [[Principal Component Analysis]] in
the first place: a $100\times100$ image is a point in 10,000-dimensional space, almost all of
which is empty, and dimensionality reduction is the only way to work in it.
[[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] owns that argument.

## In the book

Chapter of [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]], written before the deep-learning era, so its treatment is
the classical one: edge detection, region segmentation, and reconstructing a scene's geometry from
a flat projection. That last problem, inferring three dimensions from two, is genuinely
underdetermined and no amount of learning removes the ambiguity; it is resolved by assumptions
about the world (stereo, motion, shading) rather than by better filters.
